x: Network Storage source authoring treats YAML as source code for collections, endpoints, reusable logic, tests, and libraries. The backend compiler is the source of truth: local tools validate early, then sync.py --sources asks the backend to canonicalize and safely upgrade each source before upload. # File Names Local projects store source files in the matching resource folder: Prefer .yml for new files. .yaml is accepted. Typed names are preferred, but plain names inside the correct folder are supported for backwards compatibility. # Endpoint Exposure The new model uses one resource kind for callable logic: kind: endpoint . Use exposure to choose how it is used: Exposure Meaning Client call public Publicly accessible game API endpoint NetworkStorage.CallEndpoint( slug ) internal Reusable Logic, private to backend endpoint/workflow calls not directly callable by clients Public endpoints can still be called internally. Internal endpoints are reusable logic only. # Flat And Wrapper Layouts New source should be flat: resource fields live at the top level next to sourceVersion , kind , and id . The older wrapper layout is still accepted: The backend source-upgrade route can rewrite safe wrapper layouts into the flat layout. If the backend marks an upgrade unsafe, the sync tool prints a warning and leaves the file unchanged. # Routes, Rejection, And Webhooks Use canonical routes for branching and rejects. x: This guide covers installing, configuring, running, backing up and updating sbox Network Storage Server. For every configuration key see configuration.md . To connect your game see client-setup.md . Status: early preview. Releases before 1.0 may change configuration and storage formats. Keep backups. The local-owner dashboard manages projects, API keys and core settings; it does not yet have full managed-dashboard or managed project export/import parity. Resources can be pushed from the s box editor Sync Tool. # Requirements Linux (x64 or arm64), macOS (Apple Silicon or Intel) or Windows (x64) No .NET runtime needed: release binaries are self-contained SQLite needs nothing extra. PostgreSQL 13 or newer if you choose it. A port reachable by your players (8080 by default) # Local owner and management dashboard Run sbox-ns setup to choose the database and optionally create the owner with hidden password input. Leave the owner username blank to use browser setup. For scripted setup, supply --admin-username NAME --admin-password-file FILE or NS_ADMIN_USERNAME and NS_ADMIN_PASSWORD ; passwords are never accepted as command-line arguments. Password files are read relative to the current working directory, with a final newline removed. Passwords must be 12–1024 characters. Setup retains an existing account rather than overwriting it. For a remote server, the simplest first login is sbox-ns admin login-link . Run it on the server and open the printed single-use link; with no owner yet

s box Network Storage is the central server your game is missing. Your game servers, whether a player s listen server or your own dedicated box, are thin callers: currency, XP, levels, items, high scores and every other important rule run here, behind the HTTPS endpoint you control. # Player-hosted A player runs the listen server from their own game. That server only ever holds the public key ( sbox_ns_... ), so it can read shared data and call public endpoints, but every important check runs on this backend. Game collections stay endpoint-only, so a compromised host cannot rewrite player data directly. This is the cheapest way to start, and it is safe by default. # Dedicated Your own box runs the game server with a secret key ( sbox_sk_... ). It can call dedicated-only endpoints ( requiresSecretKey ) and use the management API. Players still only hold the public key in the published game. Use this for tournaments, seasons, or anything worth protecting. # Hybrid Players host day-to-day sessions while your dedicated box handles special modes. One project serves both at once: public endpoints for everyone, secret-key endpoints for your box. # Key rules The game client and any player-run host get only the project ID and the public key. The NetworkStorage.Configure line in game code uses those two values plus your base URL. x: sbox Network Storage Server reads its settings from a folder of commented TOML files. sbox-ns setup writes these files for you; this page documents every key so you can edit them by hand. Changes apply after a restart ( sbox-ns service restart , or stop and rerun sbox-ns start in the foreground). # Owner administration security The owner panel is enabled by default. sbox-ns adminpanel disable writes adminpanel.enabled = false ; restart the server to deny all owner controller endpoints, including setup, login links, login and the dashboard. Game APIs and health remain available. Restore with sbox-ns adminpanel enable or sbox-ns config set adminpanel.enabled true , then restart. Environment and conf.d overrides still take precedence over the file changed by the CLI. adminpanel.demo_read_only defaults to false. It is only for a dedicated public demonstration using an isolated SQLite database: the server seeds fixture data and supplies an ephemeral guest dashboard, rejecting owner auth/security/export, game operations and writes. Never enable it on a real operator database. adminpanel.allowed_ips is an optional comma-separated list of addresses or CIDRs, for example 127.0.0.1,::1,192.0.2.0/24 . An empty string permits all addresses. Restrictions apply before authentication and CSRF to every owner controller route. The policy uses only trusted Connection.RemoteIpAddress and never reads raw visitor headers. The server s existing forwarded-header middleware trusts only loopback prox

x: sbox-ns stores everything in one of two backends, selected by database.provider in database.toml ( sqlite or postgres only). Check the connection with sbox-ns db test and inspect versions with sbox-ns db status . Every key below is also listed in configuration.md . # Which one to choose Backend Choose it when Scaling note SQLite (default) Solo dev, a single server, or first install. Nothing to install or configure. One file, one writer machine. Fine for most single-server games. PostgreSQL 13 or newer You already operate Postgres, want the database on a separate machine, or want your provider s managed backups. Tune the pool (below). One server instance per schema; see below. ScyllaDB is not supported by this server. There is no ScyllaDB provider setting. ScyllaDB notes elsewhere in this repo describe the managed service internals, not this binary. # SQLite Everything lives in data dir /sbox-ns.db (WAL mode). No users, no passwords, no server to run. Copy the file only while the server is stopped; for live backups use sbox-ns db backup , which backs up consistently while running. Each connection opens with journal_mode=WAL and synchronous=NORMAL . WAL keeps committed transactions atomic across an application crash; NORMAL avoids a disk sync on every commit. An OS crash or power loss can lose recent commits, so use reliable local storage and keep backups. # PostgreSQL Connection fields: host , port , database , username , plus either password or password_file . x: Installable server modules: starter kits (economy, progression, inventory, leaderboards), integrity monitoring (server-side anticheat) and player insights (analytics). Modules are declarative bundles compiled into the binary : a manifest plus authored definitions. They never download code at runtime and never run outside code. # Lifecycle Catalog. The dashboard Modules page lists every embedded module with its version, description, requested permissions, the definitions it adds, and its install state. Works offline; modules.json absent means nothing is installed. Preview. Installing first shows every definition and permission. Name conflicts with existing definitions are listed and the install refuses until they are resolved. Install. Definitions are written into the live definition tables with a module ownership field under the module s id_ prefix (for example economy_earn ). The install is audited and shows a toast. Kit endpoints are public-key callable, so they work in player-hosted projects. Disable. Hooks stop, panels hide, and the module s endpoints answer ENDPOINT_DISABLED . Data and settings are kept; re-enabling restores everything without data loss. Uninstall. Requires typing the module id. Keep data converts definitions to ordinary project definitions (ownership stripped, names and records kept); delete data also removes the module s definitions, its records (ledger entries included) and its game-values items. x: The owner console has two server-wide pages next to All projects : Server ( /dashboard/server ): live CPU, memory, disk, network and request figures for this sbox-ns process and its host or container. No configuration is needed and nothing is sent anywhere unless you add a channel. # Server page The header shows the version, uptime, .NET runtime, OS and architecture, database provider, version and ping, and the data folder. The live tiles update every 500 ms by default. Pick 250 ms, 1 s, 2 s or 5 s, or pause; the choice is remembered in the browser. Each tile has a sparkline of the last 2 minutes, or of the last 15 minutes or 24 hours (one point per minute) when you change Chart . Polling pauses while the browser tab is hidden. Without JavaScript the page shows the latest sample; refresh it to update. x: sbox-ns notifies operators through channels : email over SMTP, Discord webhooks, and generic HTTP webhooks (with presets for Slack-compatible webhooks, Microsoft Teams, ntfy and Gotify). Alerts come from two sources: Captured errors , built in and always on (below). Alert rules you add in the owner console under Alerts , for example CPU use above 90 % for 2 minutes or free disk below 5 GB . Rules, metrics and the Server page are described in monitoring.md . Every send is best-effort: a failed send is logged, shown in the alert history, and never fails the request or rule check that triggered it. No channel is configured by default, and no outside service is required. # Channels Channels come from two places and are used the same way: Where Kinds Edited with alerts.toml , conf.d/ , NS_ environment variables one Discord webhook, one SMTP target sbox-ns config set , restart to apply Owner console, Alerts → Channels any number of email, Discord and webhook channels the console, live Both appear in the console s channel list; alerts.toml channels are marked and read-only there. Each console channel has: Minimum severity : info , warning , error or critical . The channel receives alerts at or above it. alerts.toml channels receive everything. Scope : all alerts (server-wide), or only alerts about one project. Project-scoped channels receive that project s captured errors only; rules watch the whole server, so their alerts go to server-wide channels. Send test sends a real notificat

x: sbox-ns mcp serves the Model Context Protocol over stdio. Your coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Claude Desktop and others) starts it on your server through SSH, or directly on your own machine. Nothing extra listens on the network, and the agent can do only what that login can do. With it, an agent can set up the server, give you the line for your game, write and validate collections and endpoints, dry-run them, read request logs and errors, and look at player records. Anything that changes or deletes definitions or data is off until you turn it on. # Connect # Server over SSH (recommended for a VPS) Other clients that read an mcpServers file: my-vps is a host from your ~/.ssh/config . Neither SSH nor sudo may ask for a password, because the agent cannot type one: use SSH key authentication, and either log in as root or allow this one command without a password ( youruser ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/bin/sbox-ns mcp via visudo ). Running as root gives every tool. Database work still runs as the sbox-ns service account, so file ownership stays correct. If you would rather not give the agent root, use sudo -u sbox-ns sbox-ns mcp : reading, testing and saving work, but config_set and service_restart fail, because the operator configuration and the system service belong to root. # Your own machine When the server runs on the same computer (development), skip SSH. x: Server releases and game-library releases are independent. Updating the backend must not require republishing an otherwise working game. Library version, package revision, game revision, API version ( v3 ) and database schema version are different identifiers; never compare them as one version. Tracking: server epic #57 and library tracker #6 . Backend/client contracts link S1 #58 ↔ L1 #7 , S3 #60 ↔ L2 #8 , and S6 #63 ↔ L3 #9 . GitHub dependency links, not prose alone, define the implementation order. # Non-breaking release rules Patch releases preserve existing request syntax, response meanings, error codes, authentication, save semantics and defaults. New fields/capabilities are additive. Follow the existing operator-version rules in releasing.md ; a server version bump does not authorize breaking the game API. A rename introduces the replacement while continuing to accept the old form. Keep actual translation logic at the API boundary; do not scatter version checks through storage/endpoint execution. Record why the old form exists and its linked deprecation issue. Do not create empty compatibility abstractions ahead of a real rename. Deprecation is a warning, not a rejection. Support a replaced library version (or API form) for at least six calendar months after its successor ships , with at least 90 days of published removal notice . The later date wins. x: Publish new game builds without breaking players on older ones. Each package sync that publishes a revision keeps an immutable snapshot of that revision s definitions; owners set support rules; the server tells each client what to do and can enforce it server-side (opt-in, off by default). # Publishing flow The editor Sync Tool pushes definitions, then POST /v3/manage/{projectId}/package-sync with the new currentRevisionId . When the revision actually changes, the server promotes staged overrides, resets revisionPublishedAt to now (the grace anchor), and writes revisions/{revisionId}.json : the full merged endpoints, workflows, collections, queries and game values plus the publish time. The write is once-only: later live edits never rewrite a snapshot. revisions/index.json records the retained ids, grace starts and owner overrides (ended/extended grace). The Versions page ( /dashboard/projects/{id}/versions ) lists live, in-grace and expired revisions with publish times, distinct players per revision (24h, from heartbeat/request identity sketches) and non-additive schema warnings. # Retention The server keeps live plus the most recent N earlier revisions ( N per project, default 3, range 0-20, set under Project → Revision policy). A revision still inside its support window is preserved even past the count; it is pruned from the index only after the window lapses. Snapshot files are definition JSON only (no player records). # Rules Per project (all unset by default; untouched
